summary: Weekly pilot sync focused on TTFT and streaming behavior across varying sequence lengths. Customer reported sporadic first-token spikes and tail microbursts under mixed live traffic. Redwood SE presented microbenchmark plan and kernel-switch recommendations; customer agreed to run seqlen-64/128 runs and enable extra logging. Next checkpoint in one week to review traces and decide on hedging policy and dedicated burst capacity.
topics: Streaming handshake vs batch path tradeoffs
KV cache behavior and prefix cache debugging
transcript:
[00:00] Sara: alright hi everyone thanks for hopping on, this is the week three latency sprint check-in for BlueNova -> Redwood pilot. quick roll call?
[00:15] Priya: hey, Priya here, Evan, Marcus and Lina on our side.
[00:21] Evan: morning all. quick note, running on k8s in GCP, node pool preemptible for dev, main service is in a dedicated VPC.
[00:30] Miguel: cool thanks. so agenda, we want to go over the ttft spikes you saw, run through a microbenchmark plan, and discuss kernel switching strategies and seqlen hedging.
[00:45] Marcus: yeah we've been seeing first token jitter - sometimes 200ms then 800ms outliers, mostly when sequence length goes above ~120 tokens.
[00:58] Lina: and we also observed an oddging microburst every ~7-10 minutes that lines up with a background batch job. might be contention on the KV cash - sorry, KV cache.
[01:12] Sara: (laughs) 'KV cash' made my Monday. ok, Miguel do you want to share the benchmark plan?
[01:20] Miguel: sure, sharing screen now - slide deck link: drive/BlueNova/pilot/benchmarks-v3, benchmark CSV: drive/BlueNova/pilot/benchmarks-micro.csv. the plan is three profiles: short (seqlen 32), medium (64/128), long (256). for each we do 1k requests 1rps baseline and also microburst tests: 100reqs at 20rps. we collect ttft, p50/p95/p99, gpu utilization and trace spans.
[01:46] Priya: ok sounds good. question — for streaming we currently do chunked responses; when the model warms kv cache the handshake seems to add 60–80ms sometimes. can you explain handshake vs batch path?
[02:00] Miguel: yeah, quick expl — streaming handshake has an extra roundtrip to init the stream and evict/attach kv state. when the runtime picks the streaming kernel path it optimizes for token-by-token but there's a per-stream setup cost. batch path uses continuous batching which has lower amortized per-token but higher latency for the very first token if batching waits. it's a tradeoff.
[02:26] Evan: so in our traffic mix — lots of short interactions then occasional long reports. what would you recommend? streaming always or hedged approach?
[02:35] Miguel: hedged strategy usually wins. attempt streaming path immediately with a short timeout (e.g., 40ms), otherwise fall back to the high-throughput batch path. that reduces TTFT regressions without blowing throughput.
[02:51] Dr. Marcus: what's the effort to change hedging parameters? we have limited ops time.
[02:58] Sara: Redwood can push a hedging config at the routing layer; it's a config flip for hosted and a small runtime flag for dedicated/private. Miguel can prepare a recommended config.
[03:08] Miguel: I'll produce recommended timeouts and knob values. also, kernel selection depends on sequence length distribution. for seqlen <=64 we prefer kernel A (low-latency single-token optimized), for 128+ kernel B (vectorized attention) tends to be better. but thresholds depend on model and quantization.
[03:30] Evan: model is rn101-mini-open (customer shorthand), quantized to 8-bit. any gotchas?
[03:36] Miguel: 8-bit quant affects kernel performance; some kernels have optimized q8 paths, others fallback and cause extra copies — that can explain p99 spikes. we'll include that in the microbench.
[03:48] Lina: we can flip quantization off for a test environment but not prod.
[03:52] Priya: can you also look at cold-start behavior? we saw a few 1s spreads after deploys.
[03:58] Miguel: yes cold-starts show up as TTFT outliers; we suspect model weight page-in and JIT/kernels warming. for dedicated infra we can pin warmed instances and keep a small warm pool to avoid that.
[04:12] Sara: quick question on observability — what's needed from your side to correlate traces?
[04:18] Evan: we'll export request ids and the sidecar traces; we need the microbenchmark CSV format and the trace ingestion template.
[04:25] Miguel: sending format now. will share a small script to annotate trace IDs. link: drive/BlueNova/pilot/trace-template.json (note: file name may be 'trace temp' in the drive, transcription may garble that).
[04:40] Priya: security — how do logs get shared? we prefer S3 with encryption and limited TTL.
[04:46] Ana: we can push artifacts to your S3 via presigned URLs or you can push to our bucket. we'll include SOC2 excerpt in the package.
[04:55] Priya: great.
[05:00] Miguel: ok next — microburst experiment specifics. for each microburst we capture GPU queue depth, kernel switch counts, and any context switch on the node. we expect to see kernel switching when sequences cross thresholds or when continuous batching merges tokens.
[05:20] Evan: how do we capture 'kernel switch counts'? is that in agent logs?
[05:26] Miguel: yes, our runtime logs a kernel_id per request and we can aggregate. we'll ask you to enable debug-level runtime logs for two hours on staging and collect.
[05:36] Lina: done, I'll enable for staging this week and share.
[05:40] Dr. Marcus: can we also sample token distributions? sometimes prompts include long system messages that bump seqlen unseen.
[05:49] Miguel: please include token-length histogram in the logs, that helps map percentiles to kernel decisions.
[05:55] Sara: ok let's talk about dedicated vs hosted pricing for this pattern — short bursts, mostly short interactions with occasional long reports.
[06:03] Priya: budget constraint — we'd prefer hosted but worried about cost during bursts. dedicated seems expensive but maybe the hedging reduces cost?
[06:12] Sara: pricing delta doc coming. high-level: hosted units billed per token with dynamic routing; dedicated is reserved GPU pools that give predictable p50/p95 but with a monthly commitment. hedging reduces lateral cost by routing some work to cheaper kernels when appropriate.
[06:28] Evan: is there a hybrid? e.g., baseline hosted, burst to dedicated?
[06:33] Miguel: yes, smart routing can overflow to dedicated or cheaper regions on spikes — we can set capacity tiers and a fallback policy.
[06:40] Priya: that might fit our procurement constraints — cheaper baseline, fallback to committed capacity. we'll need SSO/SAML and audit logs for compliance too.
[06:51] Ana: noted; I'll attach our SSO doc and audit log retention options.
[06:56] Miguel: one more item — we saw in your previous traces a few request ids with 'runtime-exec OOM' and a kernel fallback event after that. can you confirm those timestamps?
[07:06] Evan: yes, two events on Aug 28 evening window — I'll pull them.
[07:10] Miguel: great. include them in uploads so we can correlate kernel fallback vs OOM.
[07:16] Priya: what's your suggested default seqlen threshold to flip kernels?
[07:22] Miguel: starting point: <=64 -> kernel A; 65-160 -> kernel B; 161+ -> kernel C (long attention). but we'll validate with bench results; sometimes q8 models shift the breakpoints.
[07:38] Dr. Marcus: can runtime do dynamic per-request kernel selection based on predicted seqlen?
[07:44] Miguel: yes — we look at the prompt length and predict produce path at ingress; that's fast and avoids switching mid-stream. but if seqlen changes during generation we can switch with some state copy cost. that's where KV cache movement matters.
[07:57] Sara: recording note: Miguel will send bench plan and config template; Evan/Lina do logs; Ana will send security snapshots. next check: 2027-09-10 14:30 UTC internal decision checkpoint.
[08:10] Priya: quick follow-up — can we do a 30m deep dive specifically on microburst mitigation next week if bench shows persistent spikes?
[08:18] Sara: yes we'll schedule that depending on results.
[08:22] Miguel: one more technical note — in our test we saw streaming handshake cost amortized over 3 tokens; if typical responses are 1-2 tokens, streaming is inefficient. for short responses you may want hedged batch path.
[08:39] Evan: a lot of our UI calls are short (status/check) but user-generated reports are long. we can tag traffic types; is that routing key supported?
[08:47] Miguel: yes, route by route or API key, and route rules can map to hedging policies.
[08:53] Priya: any risks with the hedging approach? could it increase overall cost?
[08:57] Miguel: slight risk — duplicated work in hedged fast-fallback increases tokens if both paths run to completion; we set conservative timeouts to minimize duplicate token costs. often the p99 benefit outweighs marginal cost.
[09:12] Lina: let's talk practical: I'll enable debug logs Thursday, Evan will run the seqlen profile tests Friday and upload results.
[09:20] Sara: perfect. I'll follow up with a calendar invite and links.
[09:24] Priya: thanks everyone.
[09:27] Speaker 1: (mumbling) ok great.
[09:30] Sara: end notes — remember to include 1) request ids, 2) token histogram, 3) config snapshot of current router. Miguel will send microbench CSV and run script.
[09:45] Miguel: attaching recommended config example in the notes: hedging timeout=40ms, streaming-preference=true, seqlen-thresholds as discussed; will put exact YAML in the folder.
[09:56] Evan: any immediate blockers? procurement wants a rough TCO for both options.
[10:02] Sara: I'll send a short TCO note with expected monthly costs under three traffic shapes: baseline, bursty, and steady-report.
[10:10] Priya: perfect. meeting over.
[10:12] (call ends)

Notes: transcription contains some errors (filename/text garbling), but core action items and links were confirmed.
